title: Subject pronouns: yo, tú, usted…
summary: The words for I, you, he, she, we and they, and when to use tú or usted.
focus: Subject pronouns; tú vs usted; tú/tu and él/el
content:
## The six persons

Every Spanish verb form belongs to one of six grammatical persons. These are the subject pronouns:

| person | pronoun | English |
|---|---|---|
| 1st singular | **yo** | I |
| 2nd singular | **tú** | you (one person, informal) |
| 3rd singular | **él / ella / usted** | he / she / you (one person, formal) |
| 1st plural | **nosotros / nosotras** | we |
| 2nd plural | **vosotros / vosotras** | you (several people, informal, Spain) |
| 3rd plural | **ellos / ellas / ustedes** | they / you (several people) |

The **-as** forms (*nosotras, vosotras, ellas*) are used for groups made up only of women. A mixed group is *nosotros*, *vosotros*, *ellos*.

## Tú or usted?

Both mean *you* for one person. **Tú** is informal: friends, family, children, classmates, people your age. **Usted** is formal and respectful: strangers, older people, officials, customers, your boss on the first day.

*Usted* takes the **same verb form as él/ella**:

- *¿Tú eres de aquí?*: Are you from here? (informal)
- *¿Usted es de aquí?*: Are you from here? (formal)

In Latin America **ustedes** is the only plural *you*, formal or not. In Spain, *vosotros* is the informal plural and *ustedes* the formal one.

## Spanish usually drops the pronoun

Because the verb ending already shows the person, pronouns are mostly left out: *Soy médica* rather than *Yo soy médica*. Keep them for **emphasis** or **contrast** (*Yo soy de Madrid, ella es de Lima*) and with *usted*, where it makes the formality clear.

## Watch the accents

Two pairs of words differ only by an accent.

- **tú** (you) vs **tu** (your): *Tú tienes tu libro.*: You have your book.
- **él** (he) vs **el** (the): *Él es el profesor.*: He is the teacher.

The pronouns are the ones with the accent.

vocabulary.meaning: you all (formal, or any plural you in Latin America)

quiz.prompt: You are talking to your friend's grandmother for the first time. Which 'you' do you use?
quiz.explanation: A stranger who is older than you gets the respectful form, usted.
A group of only women is ellas.

quiz.prompt: Complete with the pronoun for 'we' (a mixed group): ___ somos estudiantes.
quiz.explanation: A mixed or all-male group is nosotros.
A classmate is informal, and the pronoun 'you' carries an accent: tú.

quiz.prompt: Usted takes the same verb form as…
quiz.explanation: Usted is grammatically third person: usted es, usted habla.

quiz.prompt: Complete: ___ es el profesor. (He is the teacher.)
quiz.explanation: 'He' is él with an accent; 'el' without accent means 'the'.

quiz.prompt: In Mexico, how do you say 'you' to a group of friends?
quiz.explanation: In Latin America ustedes is used for every plural 'you'; vosotros is mainly Spain.
hints: Latin America has one plural you.

quiz.prompt: Which sentence has the accents right?
quiz.explanation: Tú (you) has the accent, tu (your) does not.

listening.text: ¿Usted es el profesor de español, señor?
listening.meaning: Are you the Spanish teacher, sir?
listening.note: Usted takes the él/ella verb form.

listening.text: Él tiene tu libro en su mochila.
listening.meaning: He has your book in his backpack.
listening.note: Él (he) has an accent; tu (your) does not.

listening.text: Nosotras somos amigas de Marta y de Ana.
listening.meaning: We are friends of Marta and Ana.
listening.note: Nosotras: a group made up only of women.

listening.text: Ellos son mis abuelos y ella es mi tía.
listening.meaning: They are my grandparents and she is my aunt.
listening.note: New word: la tía = the aunt.

listening.text: Tú trabajas en el banco y él trabaja en la oficina.
listening.meaning: You work at the bank and he works at the office.
listening.note: New word: la oficina = the office.

conversations.title: Formal and informal
conversations.scenario: Sara meets her new manager, Señor Ruiz, and then her new colleague Diego.

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: Buenos días. ¿Usted es el señor Ruiz?
lines.meaning: Good morning. Are you Mr Ruiz?

lines.speaker: b
lines.text: Sí, soy yo. ¿Y usted es Sara?
lines.meaning: Yes, that's me. And you are Sara?

lines.speaker: a
lines.meaning: Yes, sir. Pleased to meet you.

lines.speaker: b
lines.text: Igualmente. Él es Diego, su compañero.
lines.meaning: Likewise. He is Diego, your colleague.

lines.speaker: a
lines.meaning: Hi, Diego. Are you from here?

lines.speaker: b
lines.text: No, yo soy de Santander. ¿Y tú?
lines.meaning: No, I'm from Santander. And you?

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: Yo soy de Bilbao. Nosotros somos del norte.
lines.meaning: I'm from Bilbao. We're from the north.

lines.speaker: b
lines.text: ¡Qué bien! Ellos también son del norte.
lines.meaning: Great! They're from the north too.

bites.title: Usted acts like él/ella
bites.rule: Usted means you, but grammatically it is third person, so it takes the él/ella verb form. Think 'Your Honour is…'.

bites.title: The pronoun takes the accent
bites.rule: Tú (you) and él (he) carry an accent; tu (your) and el (the) don't. The pronoun gets the accent.

bites.title: One man makes it -os
bites.rule: Nosotras, vosotras and ellas are only for all-women groups. Add a single man and it becomes nosotros, vosotros, ellos.
bites.example: Marta y Lucía → ellas. Marta y Pablo → ellos.
bites.example_meaning: Marta and Lucía → they (f). Marta and Pablo → they.

bites.title: Drop it unless it matters
bites.rule: The verb ending already says who, so Spanish usually skips yo, tú, él. Keep them for contrast or emphasis.
bites.example: Soy médica. Yo soy de Madrid, ella es de Lima.
bites.example_meaning: I'm a doctor. I'm from Madrid, she's from Lima.

sorts.title: Tú or usted?
sorts.why: Tú is for friends, family, kids and peers; usted shows respect to strangers, elders and officials.

sorts.title: Which pronoun replaces them?
sorts.why: The -as forms are only for groups of women; any mixed group takes -os.

sorts.title: Accent or no accent?
sorts.why: Pronouns carry the accent: tú = you, él = he; tu = your, el = the.

spots.why: 'You' as a pronoun needs the accent: tú.
'He' is él with an accent; el without one means 'the'.
Su madre is a third person, like usted: es.

spots.sentence: Marta y Lucía son amigas. Ellos son de Lima.
Pablo y yo somos amigos. Nosotras somos de Chile.
spots.why: Pablo makes it a mixed group, so it's nosotros.
